q: 1. Reconnaissance survey means .........
options: conducting the surveys to get the plan of the site
conducting the surveys to get contours of the site
visual inspection of the site and study of the topographical features
explain: Reconnaissance is the preliminary inspection of a site to gather information about its topography, accessibility, and general characteristics before detailed surveying begins.

q: 2. The safety of the structure can be disturbed by ...........
options: lowering or rising of water table
excavations in the immediate vicinity of the structure
mining or tunneling operations in the neighborhood
explain: Structural stability depends on the ground conditions; changes in water pressure, nearby soil removal (excavation), or underground voids (mining) can all cause settlement or failure.

q: 3. The investigation method suitable for shallow depths is .........
explain: Open excavation (trial pits) is the most direct and economical way to inspect soil strata at shallow depths, allowing for visual inspection of the soil layers.

q: 4. The bearing capacity of soil depends on
explain: The grain size, shape, and grading of soil particles directly influence internal friction and cohesion, which are primary factors in determining ultimate bearing capacity.

q: 5. The weight and fall used in standard penetrometer test to drive the cone are .......
explain: The Standard Penetration Test (SPT) uses a standard weight of 65 kg (often cited as 63.5 kg in some codes) falling from a height of 75 cm.

q: 6. The foundation in a building is provided to
options: distribute the load over a large area
increase overall stability of the structure
transmit load to the bearing surface (sub soil) at a uniform rate
explain: Foundations serve multiple structural purposes: spreading concentrated loads to prevent soil failure, ensuring stability against sliding or overturning, and ensuring uniform pressure on the subsoil.

q: 7. The soil investigation method using the penetrometers belongs to the category of .......
explain: Penetrometer tests (like SPT or CPT) are classified as sub-surface soundings because they measure the resistance of soil to the penetration of a sampler or cone.

q: 8. The failure of foundation of a building is due to
options: lateral escape of the supporting material
explain: Foundation failure can occur physically (lateral escape of soil), chemically/environmentally (moisture changes causing shrinkage), or structurally (uneven settlement leading to cracks).

q: 9. The number of blows recorded in a standard penetration test is for a penetration of .......
explain: The 'N' value in an SPT test is the number of blows required to drive the sampler for the last 30 cm of a 45 cm total penetration.

q: 10. The safe bearing capacity of the soil is equal to
options: ultimate bearing power / factor of safety
ultimate tensile strength / factor of safety
ultimate compressive strength / factor of safety
explain: Safe Bearing Capacity (SBC) is calculated by dividing the Ultimate Bearing Capacity (the maximum pressure soil can take before shear failure) by a Factor of Safety (usually 2.5 to 3).

q: 11. The safe bearing capacity of the soil can be improved by ...........
options: draining the soil if water table is very near the base of the footing
explain: Bearing capacity can be increased by reaching stiffer strata (depth), filling voids (grouting), or removing pore water pressure (drainage).

q: 12. The bearing capacity of soils can be improved by
options: ramming the granular material like crushed stone in the soil
explain: Soil strength improves with depth (confinement), reduction of pore water pressure (drainage), and densification through the addition/compaction of granular materials.

q: 13. In a static penetrometer test the angle of the penetrating cone is ..........
explain: The standard cone used in static (Dutch) cone penetration tests has a base area of 10 cm² and an apex angle of 60°.

q: 14. The minimum depth of foundation for buildings on clays is
explain: For clayey soils, foundations must be deep enough (typically 0.9m to 1.6m) to reach beyond the 'active zone' where seasonal moisture changes cause significant swelling and shrinkage.

q: 15. Soil investigation at a site are carried out to obtain the information regarding .........
options: the engineering and the physical properties of the soils
the details of the soil profile to considerable depth
the depth to ground water table and its seasonal fluctuations
explain: Comprehensive soil reports must include soil classification (properties), the sequence of layers (profile), and hydrological data (water table).

q: 16. The raft foundations are generally used when the required area of footing is ........ the total area of the structure.
explain: If individual footings would cover more than 50% (one-half) of the building area, a continuous raft (mat) foundation becomes more economical and effective at reducing differential settlement.

q: 17. In the case of soil investigation by boring, the record of soil samples arranged according the depth where they are found is known as .........
explain: A bore-log is a technical record that provides a detailed description of the soil layers encountered at various depths during a boring operation.

q: 18. In combined footing
options: centre of gravity of the column loads must coincide with the centre of gravity of the footing
explain: To ensure uniform soil pressure distribution under a combined footing, the geometric center (C.G.) of the footing must align with the resultant C.G. of the two column loads.

q: 19. The plate loading test gives .........
options: the ultimate bearing capacity of the soil
safe bearing capacity of the soil
explain: The plate load test is used to determine the ultimate bearing capacity of soil at a specific depth and to estimate the likely settlement under a given load.

q: 20. The relationship between the ultimate bearing capacity (qu), the net ultimate bearing capacity (qnu) and the depth of footing D (r being the unit weight of the soil) is:
explain: Ultimate bearing capacity (qu) is the sum of the net ultimate bearing capacity (qnu) and the overburden pressure (γD or rD).

q: 21. The maximum load on the wooden pile should not exceed
explain: For standard timber piles, the safe design load is generally capped at 200 kN (approx. 20 tonnes) to prevent structural crushing of the wood fibers under sustained architectural loads.

q: 22. According to Rankine's theory, the minimum depth of foundation is given by .........
explain: Rankine's formula for minimum depth ensures the soil won't heave around the foundation; it uses the ratio of vertical to horizontal pressure squared.

q: 23. The minimum depth of foundation below the ground level in any soil is .........
explain: In general practice and to avoid frost action or surface disturbances, the minimum recommended depth for any foundation is 80 cm to 90 cm.

q: 24. The method of protecting the foundations in loose soils from caving in, is called
explain: Both timbering (planking and strutting) and shoring are used to provide temporary support to the sides of excavations in unstable soil.

q: 25. According to Rankine's formula, the minimum depth of foundation should be
explain: Rankine's formula for minimum depth (h) is $h =  rac{p}{w} \left(  rac{1-\sin\phi}{1+\sin\phi} ight)^2$. It ensures the weight of the soil at that depth provides enough lateral pressure to prevent the soil under the footing from heaving.

q: 26. The minimum depth of foundation for the load bearing wall of a building is restricted to
explain: For load-bearing masonry walls in standard climatic conditions, 900 mm is the widely accepted minimum depth to ensure the foundation sits below the frost line and the zone of seasonal moisture variation.

q: 27. Osmosis is .........
options: an electrical process where fine grained cohesive soils are drained using electricity
a method to determine the depth to water table
explain: Electro-osmosis is a technique used to drain water from low-permeability soils like clay by applying a direct current between electrodes.

q: 28. The approximate bearing capacity of a sound rock without any defects may be taken as .........
explain: Hard, sound rocks like granite or limestone have very high bearing capacities, typically ranging from 300 to 350 t/m².

q: 29. When two or more footing are connected by a beam, is called
explain: A strap footing (or cantilever footing) consists of two individual footings connected by a structural 'strap' beam. This is often used when one footing is placed against a property line.

q: 30. Which of the following has the lowest bearing capacity?
explain: Moist or soft clay has very little internal friction and gains its strength only from cohesion, making it significantly weaker than sands or gravels.

q: 31. The type of foundation recommended for heavily loaded steel stanchions in soils with poor bearing capacity
explain: Grillage foundations are specifically designed to spread heavy concentrated loads from steel columns over a large area using layers of steel beams.

q: 32. Well foundation is also known as .........
explain: A well foundation is a type of deep foundation, often used for bridges, which is technically referred to as a caisson.

q: 33. The most commonly used deep foundation in buildings .........
explain: Pile foundations are the most common deep foundation used for building structures to transfer loads to deeper, more stable soil layers.

q: 34. If the load coming on to a pile is transferred to a suitable bearing stratum at its bottom end, then it is called .........
explain: An end-bearing pile transfers the structural load directly through its tip to a hard, incompressible layer of rock or dense gravel.

q: 35. If the load coming on to a pile is resisted by friction developed between the surface area of the pile and the surrounding material, then it is called .........
explain: Friction piles derive their carrying capacity from the skin friction (adhesion) between the pile surface and the surrounding soil.

q: 36. Type of foundation most suitable for bridges is
explain: Pile foundations are ideal for bridges because they can reach deep, stable soil layers or bedrock, bypassing erodible riverbed material (scour) that would undermine shallower foundations.

q: 37. A pile which by itself does not carry any load but improves the bearing capacity of the soil is called .........
explain: Compaction piles are driven into loose granular soils to increase the soil's density (compactness) through vibration and displacement.

q: 38. A pile commonly used to reduce seepage and control the uplift pressures under hydraulic structure is known as .........
explain: Sheet piles are thin, interlocking plates driven into the ground to create a continuous barrier (cutoff wall) to prevent water seepage under dams or weirs.

q: 39. A pile which has an enlarged shape at the base is called .......
explain: A Franki pile (or pressure-injected foot pile) is characterized by a bulbous, enlarged base that provides high end-bearing resistance.

q: 40. A cast-in-situ concrete pile with one or more enlarged bulbs on its stem is called .........
explain: Under-reamed piles are bored cast-in-situ piles with one or more bulbs (reams) to provide better anchorage, especially in expansive soils like black cotton soil.

q: 41. Minimum depth of foundation on clayey soils
explain: Clayey soils are highly expansive. A minimum depth of 90 cm is required to ensure the footing rests below the 'active zone' where moisture changes cause the soil to shrink or swell.

q: 42. The distance between the flanges of the beams in any tier of a grillage foundation should be equal to .........
options: one and half times the flange width or 30 cm whichever is less
explain: To ensure proper concrete placement and compaction between the steel beams, a spacing of 1.5 to 2 times the flange width (or roughly 30cm) is maintained.

q: 43. Bearing capacity of soils cannot be improved by
explain: Watering the surface usually softens the soil and increases pore water pressure, which actually reduces the shear strength and bearing capacity rather than improving it.

q: 44. The maximum permissible differential settlement in the case of foundations on sandy soils is generally about ..........
explain: For isolated foundations on sand, the allowable differential settlement is restricted to 25 mm to prevent structural cracking.

q: 45. The maximum permissible differential settlement in the case of foundations on clayey soils is generally about ...........
explain: Clayey soils allow for a higher differential settlement (40 mm) because the settlement process is slower and more uniform over time compared to sand.

q: 46. The bearing capacity of water logged soil, may be improved by
explain: For waterlogged soil, the most effective first step is drainage. Removing excess water reduces pore pressure and increases the effective stress (and thus strength) of the soil grains.

q: 47. The maximum permissible total settlement in the case of raft foundations clayey soils is generally about ...........
explain: Raft foundations distribute loads over a larger area; in clay, a total settlement of up to 100 mm is often considered the permissible limit.

q: 48. The maximum permissible total settlement in the case of raft foundations sandy soils is generally about ...........
explain: For rafts on sand, the allowable total settlement is usually limited to 65 mm (standard range 40–65 mm) to ensure stability.

q: 49. Uniform distribution of loads from walls on piles is achieved by connecting the group of piles supporting the structure ...........
options: by tie rods at the bottom of the piles
by tie rods at the top of the piles
isolating the piles without any connection
explain: A pile cap (often in the form of a reinforced concrete beam) is used to tie the piles together and distribute the wall load evenly among them.

q: 50. The offsets in the stepped strip footing in brick masonry is ..........
explain: In standard brick masonry footings, the horizontal offset for each step is typically half a brick length (approx. 5 cm to 10 cm, with 5 cm being the minimum for stability).
